```{.r .cell-code}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, error = TRUE)

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(PxWebApiData)
library(scales)
library(ggridges)
library(MetBrewer)

df1 <- NULL
tryCatch({
  raw <- ApiData(
    "https://data.ssb.no/api/v0/no/table/08771",
    NACE2007 = TRUE,
    ContentsCode = TRUE,
    Tid = list(filter = "top", values = 40)
  )
  tmp          <- raw[[1]]
  time_col     <- "kvartal"
  value_col    <- "value"
  series_col   <- "næring (SN2007)"
  measure_col  <- "statistikkvariabel"
  df1 <- tmp |>
    mutate(
      value    = as.numeric(.data[[value_col]]),
      time_str = .data[[time_col]],
      date     = case_when(
        stringr::str_detect(time_str, "M") ~ lubridate::ym(sub("M", "-", time_str)),
        stringr::str_detect(time_str, "K") ~ lubridate::yq(sub("K", " Q", time_str)),
        nchar(time_str) == 4               ~ lubridate::ymd(paste0(time_str, "-01-01")),
        TRUE ~ NA_Date_
      )
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(value), !is.na(date))
}, error = function(e) message("Fetch failed: ", e$message))

if (is.null(df1) || nrow(df1) == 0) { message("No data returned for df1"); df1 <- NULL }

df2 <- NULL
tryCatch({
  raw <- ApiData(
    "https://data.ssb.no/api/v0/no/table/10634",

  tmp          <- raw[[1]]
  time_col     <- "år"
  value_col    <- "value"
  series_col   <- "hovedlovbruddstype"
  measure_col  <- "statistikkvariabel"
  df2 <- tmp |>
    mutate(

      date     = case_when(

        stringr::str_detect(time_str, "K") ~ lubridate::yq(sub("K", " Q", time_str)),
        nchar(time_str) == 4               ~ lubridate::ymd(paste0(time_str, "-01-01")),
        TRUE ~ NA_Date_
      )
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(value), !is.na(date))
}, error = function(e) message("Fetch failed: ", e$message))

if (is.null(df2) || nrow(df2) == 0) { message("No data returned for df2"); df2 <- NULL }
```

## When Three Trends Converge

Norway is simultaneously navigating a softening labour market, persistent pressures on its criminal justice system, and demographic projections that hinge critically on immigration assumptions. Taken separately, each of these dynamics tells a partial story. Viewed together, they outline something more consequential: a social infrastructure that is being tested from multiple directions at once. This post draws on Statistics Norway data to map the contours of that pressure.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# ── Initialize all derived variables ──────────────────────────────────────────
df1_vacancies    <- NULL
df1_pct          <- NULL
df1_top_sectors  <- NULL
df1_heatmap      <- NULL
df2_national     <- NULL
df2_rate         <- NULL
df2_offence_top  <- NULL
df3_scenarios    <- NULL
df3_immig        <- NULL
df3_age_total    <- NULL

# ── df1: job vacancies by sector ──────────────────────────────────────────────
if (!is.null(df1) && nrow(df1) > 0) {
  # Absolute vacancies
  df1_vacancies <- df1 |>
    filter(.data[["statistikkvariabel"]] == "Ledige stillingar") |>
    filter(!is.na(value))

  # Percentage vacancies
  df1_pct <- df1 |>
    filter(.data[["statistikkvariabel"]] == "Ledige stillingar (prosent)") |>
    filter(!is.na(value))

  # Identify top sectors by mean vacancies for focus charts
  if (nrow(df1_vacancies) > 0) {
    top_s <- df1_vacancies |>
      group_by(.data[["næring (SN2007)"]]) |>
      summarise(mean_val = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
      arrange(desc(mean_val)) |>
      slice_head(n = 8) |>
      pull("næring (SN2007)")

    df1_top_sectors <- df1_vacancies |>
      filter(.data[["næring (SN2007)"]] %in% top_s)

    # Latest quarter lollipop data
    latest_q <- max(df1_vacancies$date, na.rm = TRUE)
    df1_heatmap <- df1_vacancies |>
      filter(.data[["næring (SN2007)"]] %in% top_s) |>
      mutate(year  = lubridate::year(date),
             qtr   = paste0("Q", lubridate::quarter(date))) |>
      group_by(.data[["næring (SN2007)"]], year) |>
      summarise(mean_val = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
  }
}

# ── df2: criminal convictions ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
if (!is.null(df2) && nrow(df2) > 0) {
  # National total (filter out sub-regional rows if region col exists)
  region_col2 <- if ("region" %in% names(df2)) "region" else NULL

  df2_national <- df2 |>
    filter(.data[["statistikkvariabel"]] == "Straffede personer")
  # fixed: pipe syntax error - replaced `{ if (...) filter(...) else . }` with proper if statement after pipe
  if (!is.null(region_col2)) {
    df2_national <- df2_national |>
      filter(.data[[region_col2]] == unique(.data[[region_col2]])[1])
  }
  df2_national <- df2_national |>
    filter(!is.na(value))

  df2_rate <- df2 |>
    filter(.data[["statistikkvariabel"]] == "Straffede personer per 1000 innbyggere")
  # fixed: pipe syntax error - replaced `{ if (...) filter(...) else . }` with proper if statement after pipe
  if (!is.null(region_col2)) {
    df2_rate <- df2_rate |>
      filter(.data[[region_col2]] == unique(.data[[region_col2]])[1])
  }
  df2_rate <- df2_rate |>
    filter(!is.na(value))

  # Top offence types by total convictions across all years
  if (nrow(df2_national) > 0) {
    top_off <- df2_national |>
      group_by(.data[["hovedlovbruddstype"]]) |>
      summarise(total = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
      arrange(desc(total)) |>
      slice_head(n = 8) |>
      pull("hovedlovbruddstype")

    df2_offence_top <- df2_national |>
      filter(.data[["hovedlovbruddstype"]] %in% top_off)
  }
}

# ── df3: population projections ───────────────────────────────────────────────
if (!is.null(df3) && nrow(df3) > 0) {
  age_col3     <- if ("alder" %in% names(df3)) "alder" else NULL
  gender_col3  <- if ("kjønn" %in% names(df3)) "kjønn" else
                  if ("kjonn" %in% names(df3))  "kjonn" else NULL

  # Three main national-level scenarios: MMMM, LLML, HHMH
  target_scenarios <- c(
    "Middels nasjonal vekst (Alternativ MMMM)",
    "Lav nasjonal vekst (Alternativ LLML)",
    "Høy nasjonal vekst (Alternativ HHMH)"
  )

  df3_scenarios <- df3 |>
    filter(.data[["alternativ"]] %in% target_scenarios) |>
    filter(!is.na(value))

  # High immigration scenario specifically
  df3_immig <- df3 |>
    filter(.data[["alternativ"]] == "Høy innvandring (Alternativ MMMH)") |>
    filter(!is.na(value))

  # Aggregate total population by scenario and year (sum across age/gender)
  if (nrow(df3_scenarios) > 0) {
    df3_age_total <- df3_scenarios |>
      group_by(date, .data[["alternativ"]]) |>
      summarise(total_pop = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
      filter(total_pop > 0)
  }
}
```

## The Job Vacancy Landscape: Which Sectors Are Pulling Back?

Quarterly job vacancy data from Statistics Norway tracks not just overall labour demand, but which corners of the economy are tightening or loosening. The distribution of vacancies across sectors carries implications for where workers — including newly arrived immigrants — can find a foothold, and where shortfalls in labour supply might strain public services.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
if (exists("df1_heatmap") && !is.null(df1_heatmap) && nrow(df1_heatmap) > 0) {

  pal_heat <- met.brewer("Hiroshige", n = 10, type = "continuous")

  sector_var <- "næring (SN2007)"

  p <- df1_heatmap |>
    mutate(sector_short = str_wrap(.data[[sector_var]], width = 30)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = sector_short, fill = mean_val)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
    scale_fill_gradientn(
      colours  = pal_heat,
      labels   = comma,
      name     = "Mean vacancies"
    ) +
    labs(
      title    = "Job vacancies by sector and year",
      subtitle = "Annual mean of quarterly vacancy counts for top 8 sectors by average vacancy level",
      caption  = "Source: Statistics Norway, table 08771",
      x        = NULL,
      y        = NULL
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 9),
      axis.text.y      = element_text(size = 8),
      legend.position  = "right",
      panel.grid       = element_blank(),
      plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
      plot.subtitle    = element_text(size = 10, colour = "grey40"),
      plot.caption     = element_text(size = 8, colour = "grey50")
    )

  print(p) # fixed: missing print() statement

  peak_row <- df1_heatmap |>
    filter(mean_val == max(mean_val, na.rm = TRUE))
  low_row  <- df1_heatmap |>
    filter(mean_val == min(mean_val, na.rm = TRUE))

  cat(sprintf(
    "\nThe sector with the highest annual mean vacancy count was **%s** in **%d** (%s vacancies). The lowest recorded annual mean was in **%s** in **%d** (%s vacancies).\n\n",
    peak_row[[sector_var]][1], peak_row$year[1], comma(round(peak_row$mean_val[1])),
    low_row[[sector_var]][1],  low_row$year[1],  comma(round(low_row$mean_val[1]))
  ))

} else {
  cat("\n*Figure omitted — Statistics Norway returned no data for this series.*\n\n")
}
```

## Convictions by Offence: What the Criminal Justice Data Reveals

The number of people convicted per thousand inhabitants is one of the clearest signals of criminal justice system load. When that rate shifts across different offence categories over time, it raises questions about enforcement priorities, social conditions, and the capacity of courts and corrections to respond. The ridgeline chart below shows the distribution of conviction rates across offence types over the available years.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
if (exists("df2_offence_top") && !is.null(df2_offence_top) && nrow(df2_offence_top) > 0) {

  offence_var <- "hovedlovbruddstype"

  p <- df2_offence_top |>
    mutate(offence_wrap = str_wrap(.data[[offence_var]], width = 28),
           year_num     = lubridate::year(date)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = value, y = offence_wrap, fill = offence_wrap)) +
    geom_density_ridges(
      alpha       = 0.75,
      scale       = 1.2,
      bandwidth   = NULL,
      colour      = "white",
      linewidth   = 0.4
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = met.brewer("Klimt", n = length(unique(df2_offence_top[[offence_var]])),
                          type = "discrete"),
      guide  = "none"
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
    labs(
      title    = "Distribution of convictions across major offence categories",
      subtitle = "Density of annual conviction counts for the eight most prevalent offence types",
      caption  = "Source: Statistics Norway, table 10634",
      x        = "Convicted persons",
      y        = NULL
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      axis.text.y    = element_text(size = 8),
      panel.grid     = element_blank(),
      plot.title     = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
      plot.subtitle  = element_text(size = 10, colour = "grey40"),
      plot.caption   = element_text(size = 8, colour = "grey50")
    )

  print(p) # fixed: missing print() statement

  by_offence <- df2_offence_top |>
    group_by(.data[[offence_var]]) |>
    summarise(total = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(total))

  cat(sprintf(
    "\nAcross all available years, **%s** accumulated the highest total conviction count (%s). The offence category with the fewest total convictions among the top eight was **%s** (%s).\n\n",
    by_offence[[offence_var]][1], comma(by_offence$total[1]),
    by_offence[[offence_var]][nrow(by_offence)], comma(by_offence$total[nrow(by_offence)])
  ))

} else {
  cat("\n*Figure omitted — Statistics Norway returned no data for this series.*\n\n")
}
```

## Population Projections: How Much Depends on Immigration?

Statistics Norway publishes several demographic scenarios for Norway's future population, differing in assumptions about fertility, mortality, internal migration, and immigration. The gap between the low- and high-growth scenarios widens substantially over time, with immigration assumptions driving much of that divergence. The chart below traces the total projected population under three national-level scenarios — medium, low, and high growth — and highlights how much the long-run outlook can shift depending on which assumptions prove correct.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
if (exists("df3_age_total") && !is.null(df3_age_total) && nrow(df3_age_total) > 0) {

  scenario_var <- "alternativ"

  scenario_labels <- c(
    "Middels nasjonal vekst (Alternativ MMMM)" = "Medium growth (MMMM)",
    "Lav nasjonal vekst (Alternativ LLML)"     = "Low growth (LLML)",
    "Høy nasjonal vekst (Alternativ HHMH)"     = "High growth (HHMH)"
  )

  df3_plot <- df3_age_total |>
    mutate(scenario_label = recode(.data[[scenario_var]], !!!scenario_labels))

  pal_proj <- c(
    "Medium growth (MMMM)" = "#4e79a7",
    "Low growth (LLML)"    = "#e15759",
    "High growth (HHMH)"   = "#59a14f"
  )

  # Latest year in data
  latest_proj <- max(df3_plot$date, na.rm = TRUE)
  # Find spread at latest year
  latest_spread <- df3_plot |>
    filter(date == latest_proj) |>
    arrange(desc(total_pop))

  p <- df3_plot |>
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = total_pop, colour = scenario_label, group = scenario_label)) +
    geom_ribbon(
      data = df3_plot |>
        select(date, scenario_label, total_pop) |>
        pivot_wider(names_from = scenario_label, values_from = total_pop) |>
        filter(!is.na(`Low growth (LLML)`) & !is.na(`High growth (HHMH)`)),
      aes(ymin = `Low growth (LLML)`, ymax = `High growth (HHMH)`,
          x = date, y = NULL, colour = NULL),
      fill  = "grey80",
      alpha = 0.35,
      inherit.aes = FALSE
    ) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, alpha = 0.9) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = pal_proj, name = "Scenario") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M", accuracy = 0.1)) +
    scale_x_date(date_breaks = "5 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
    labs(
      title    = "Norway's projected total population under three national growth scenarios",
      subtitle = "Shaded band shows the range between low and high growth projections; lines trace each scenario over time",
      caption  = "Source: Statistics Norway, table 09481",
      x        = NULL,
      y        = "Total population"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      legend.position  = "top",
      legend.text      = element_text(size = 9),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey92", linewidth = 0.4),
      plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
      plot.subtitle    = element_text(size = 10, colour = "grey40"),
      plot.caption     = element_text(size = 8, colour = "grey50")
    )

  print(p) # fixed: missing print() statement

  if (nrow(latest_spread) >= 2) {
    high_val <- latest_spread$total_pop[1]
    low_val  <- latest_spread$total_pop[nrow(latest_spread)]
    gap      <- high_val - low_val
    cat(sprintf(
      "\nBy **%s**, the projected population spans from **%s** (low growth) to **%s** (high growth) — a difference of **%s** people depending on which demographic assumptions prevail.\n\n",
      format(latest_proj, "%Y"),
      label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = " million", accuracy = 0.01)(low_val),
      label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = " million", accuracy = 0.01)(high_val),
      comma(round(gap))
    ))
  }

} else {
  cat("\n*Figure omitted — Statistics Norway returned no data for this series.*\n\n")
}
```

## The Triangle Closes

What links these three datasets is not coincidence but structural interdependence. The scale and composition of immigration shapes both the labour supply that employers draw upon to fill vacancies and the demographic base over which criminal justice costs are spread. How the vacancy landscape evolves across sectors will influence where newcomers can integrate economically. And how the conviction rate changes across offence types signals whether the social integration of a rapidly changing population is proceeding smoothly or encountering friction. Norway is not unique in facing these pressures — but the precision of its statistical infrastructure, and the willingness to project scenarios honestly across a wide range of assumptions, places it in a stronger position than most to anticipate and respond to what comes next.
